[Question - Mechanical/Materials Sciences] Are shorter pieces of 2x4 wood(usually pine) better than longer pieces when comparing strength and warping?

This is true with all things. The longer something is the easier it is to bend. Not always is that a bad thing, though. Like with sky scrapers, the ability to bend and sway is actually better and provides more stability.

With that being said, if the project calls for something not having any sway, (like a deck, shed, etc) then it's better to use long pieces and reinforce it with more studs or posts. The general rule is to have a stud/post every 3-5 feet depending on if you are using 2x4, 4x4, 2x6, etc. Obviously using a 4x4 will be stronger than a 2x4.

The best way to prevent warping is to use pressure treated wood and use more supports. If the project calls for something to be long without support, it's best to use smaller pieces and layer them together.

One little correction. 2x4 and 2x6 are set 16" apart. 2x8 to 2x12 can go 24" apart. Also blocking and sheeting will help keep a wall rigid. But your best option is to allow your lumber to acclimate to the average humidity first as this will counteract any surprise shrinking or expanding.

If the project calls for something to be long without support, it's best to use smaller pieces and layer them together.

Just to add to this: I was always taught that layering smaller boards together was better because (A) it was cheaper, and (B) they would warp in different directions, causing the overall structure to reinforce against itself. Not sure if it's 100% true, but it makes sense.

Are you talking about warping due to heat and moisture, or due to stress?

A longer piece of wood will warp more if pressure (stress) is applied on one end. (Think of how a short lever bends compared to a long lever)

If we are talking about warping due to the elements, both a long and short stud will warp the same. What is happening is, the fiberous strands that make up the wood expand and contract. This happens on a tiny scale. So it doesn't matter if the piece is long or short, because the wood is being changed on a microscopic level overall. These microscopic changes add up over the length of a board.

So, we have to ask the question. Are we measuring warp as a matter of ratio (deviation:length) or are we measuring warp as a matter of just how much deviation overall. If we are measuring by ratio, a long and short stud will be the same. But if we are just measuring deviation, the longer stud will have more deviation compared to the short stud.
